device: Japanese-market LED ceiling lights (シーリングライト), infrared remote control
status: Desk research only. No code has been sent to a real lamp. Labels: [docs] = manufacturer or chip-vendor document; [community] = blog, GitHub or forum; [inferred] = derived in this research (bit reversal, XOR rule, pattern); [unknown] = no public data found.

conventions.byteNotation: Every hex string in 'commands', 'frames' and 'searchCandidates' lists the bytes in the order they are sent, and each byte is sent LSB-first (bit0 first). This is the native AEHA and NEC convention. hello-ino, shrkn65, katsumin, widehill, negligible, IRRC32 and Flipper's address/command fields all use it. Where a source uses another notation, the entry quotes that source's string in 'commandsAsGiven' or 'customerCodeAsGiven'.

conversions.ArduinoIRremote_v3plus: decodedRawData is the first 4 bytes joined little-endian (2C 52 09 2C -> 0x2C09522C). The mamezou article writes the 5th byte separately in parentheses: 0x2C09522C(0x25).
conversions.MSB-first tools (IRremote v2 'value', IR: Bit-reverse every byte: 2C->34, 52->4A, 09->90, 01->80, 10->08. In this notation the Panasonic lighting customer code is 0x344A and Hitachi's is 0x8008. ESPHome AEHA encode() masks from 1<<15 (address) and 1<<7 (data) down, i.e. MSB-first [community: esphome aeha_protocol.cpp].
conversions.ESPHome_transmit_nec: Sends 16-bit fields LSB-first: address = b0 | b1<<8 (82 6D -> 0x6D82), command = b2 | b3<<8 (BE 41 -> 0x41BE) [community: esphome nec_protocol.cpp].
conversions.Flipper_NECext: address: 'b0 b1 00 00', command: 'b2 b3 00 00' (for example address 82 6D 00 00, command BE 41 00 00). Flipper uses NECext whenever byte1 is not ~byte0. That is the case for every Japanese lighting NEC code here [inferred from the Flipper NEC decoder logic].
conversions.katsumin_M5Stack_decoder: Prints the AEHA customer code as a 16-bit little-endian value (2C 52 -> 522C; 01 10 -> 1001).

NEC.frameLayout: custom code byte0, custom code byte1, command, ~command. All bytes LSB-first. Every Japanese ceiling-light code found uses an EXTENDED 16-bit custom code, so byte1 is not ~byte0.
NEC.repeat: While a key is held, a repeat code (9000 on, 2250 off, 562.5 on) is sent every 108 ms. Some lighting remotes (Takizumi) resend the full frame instead.
NEC.measuredInWild: Captures run about 7-12% long: Broadlink about 9.7/4.8 ms leader, TSOP4838 on a Toshiba remote about 10.15/5.0 ms with 650-700 us marks. Decode by ratio, not by absolute time.
NEC.source: https://akizukidenshi.com/goodsaffix/OE13KIR.pdf [docs: Akizuki NEC-format transmitter sheet: 9 ms + 4.5 ms leader, 0.56/1.125/2.25 ms, 108 ms, 38 kHz, LSB first]; https://www.alldatasheet.com/datasheet-pdf/pdf/6958/NEC/UPD6121.html [docs: NEC uPD6121/6122, origin of the format, '9-ms carrier + 4.5-ms OFF' leader, custom codes assigned by NEC]; https://www.sbprojects.net/knowledge/ir/nec.php [community: gives 560 us and a 110 ms repeat]; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/esphome/esphome/dev/esphome/components/remote_base/nec_protocol.cpp [community: 9000/4500/560/1690/560, 108000 repeat period]

AEHA.aka: 家製協 / 家電協 format of the Association for Electric Home Appliances (家電製品協会). Called 'Kaseikyo' (romanised 家製協) by hifi-remote, Arduino-IRremote and Flipper, which implement only the 48-bit member.
AEHA.frameLayout: Bytes 0-1: 16-bit customer (maker) code. Byte 2: low nibble = parity (XOR of the 4 customer-code nibbles), high nibble = system/data0. Then variable-length data, often ending in an XOR checksum. All LSB-first. Parity check: Panasonic lighting 2C 52 -> C^2^2^5 = 9 -> byte2 = x9. Hitachi 01 10 -> 0 -> byte2 = x0. Sharp AV AA 5A -> F -> 8F. Panasonic AV 02 20 -> 0 -> B0 [inferred, consistent with all sources].
AEHA.repeat: Usually no repeat code: the whole frame is resent about every 130 ms while the key is held. Panasonic lighting remotes send each frame twice per press, about 75 ms apart.
AEHA.source: http://elm-chan.org/docs/ir_format.html [community: T=350-500 us (425 typ), 33-40 kHz (38 typ), 16-bit customer + 4-bit parity, about 130 ms repeat]; http://shrkn65.nobody.jp/remocon/aeha.html [community: leader 8T/4T, 0=1T/1T, 1=1T/3T, trailer 1T + >=8 ms, 33-40 kHz recommended]; https://hello-ino.seesaa.net/article/2012-10-17.html [community: T=425 (350-500), LSB-first]; https://renesas.com/jp/ja/document/apn/874436 [docs: Renesas R01AN1266JJ0103 RL78 'リモコン受信処理（家製協フォーマット）', header + 48-bit data stored LSB-first]; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/esphome/esphome/dev/esphome/components/remote_base/aeha_protocol.cpp [community: BITWISE=425, header 8T/4T, 1=1T/3T, data 2-35 bytes, MSB-first!]

Kaseikyo48_relation.summary: Kaseikyo is AEHA fixed at 48 bits: 16-bit vendor ID, 4-bit vendor parity, then data, then an XOR checksum. Arduino-IRremote uses KASEIKYO_UNIT 432 us (3456/1728 header, 1296 one-space, 130 ms repeat). Its vendor IDs (little-endian of the transmitted bytes) are Panasonic 0x2002 (bytes 02 20), Denon 0x3254, Mitsubishi 0xCB23, Sharp 0x5AAA (bytes AA 5A) and JVC 0x0103. Flipper's Kaseikyo decoder needs exactly 48 bits, vendor_id = data[0] | data[1]<<8, a vendor-parity nibble check and data[5] == data[2]^data[3]^data[4]. hifi-remote IRP: {37k,432}<1,-1|1,-3>(8,-4,M:8,N:8,X:4,D:4,S:8,F:8,E:4,C:4,1,-173)+, Panasonic = OEM 2.32.
Kaseikyo48_relation.consequenceForLights: Panasonic lighting frames are 40-bit AEHA (vendor bytes 2C 52 = 0x522C) and Hitachi lighting frames are 88-bit AEHA (vendor 01 10). Neither is Kaseikyo-48. Flipper stores them RAW (Flipper-IRDB HK9494 file is raw). IRremoteESP8266 reports UNKNOWN ('42 bits' = rawlen/2 for an 83-edge, 40-bit frame). Arduino-IRremote reports a generic PulseDistance protocol. ESPHome transmit_aeha can send them only after bit-reversing every byte.
Kaseikyo48_relation.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Arduino-IRremote/Arduino-IRremote/master/src/ir_Kaseikyo.hpp [community]; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flipperdevices/flipperzero-firmware/dev/lib/infrared/encoder_decoder/kaseikyo/infrared_decoder_kaseikyo.c [community]; https://hifi-remote.com/wiki/index.php/Kaseikyo [community]; https://qiita.com/ayakix/items/3ad454f135fb63a92026 [community: ceiling light = IRremoteESP8266 UNKNOWN 42 bits, rawData[83] starting 3486,1722,446,418]

brands.customerCode: 0x2C52 = bytes 2C 52 (LSB-first). VERIFIED by 7 independent sources plus the AEHA parity nibble 9.
brands.frameLayout: 2C 52 | S9 | CMD | S9^CMD. S9 = 0x09 for basic keys and 0x39 for colour, timer and channel-confirm keys (system nibble 0 vs 3). Last byte = byte2 XOR byte3.
brands.channels: CH1-CH3 (most remotes: HK9327K, HK9392K, HK9478, HK9482, HK9484, HK9490, HK9492, HK9493, HK9494, HK9496, HK9497, HK9800). HK9339 ON/OFF remote has CH1-2. Wall switches WH7215K/WTC56919 use CH A-C.
brands.channelRule: Basic keys: CMD = 0x20 + 8*ch + k, where ch is 1..3 and k is 2 明るく, 3 暗く, 4 全灯, 5 点灯/お好み/省エネ, 6 常夜灯, 7 消灯. CH1 = 0x2A-0x2F, CH2 = 0x32-0x37, CH3 = 0x3A-0x3F. Colour keys (byte2 = 0x39): CMD = 0x90 + 4*(ch-1) + (warm ? 1 : 0).

learningNotes: WHAT A 38 kHz DEMODULATING RECEIVER SEES (M5Stack Unit IR U002: 38 kHz hardware-demodulating receiver plus 940 nm LED, range <= 5 m [docs]). On a Cardputer Grove port, IR_TX (yellow) = G2 and IR_RX (white) = G1 [docs, inferred from wire colours]; the built-in TX is G44. The receiver outputs the mark/space envelope only; the carrier frequency is lost and the output is inverted (active-low) [docs: Akizuki sheet]. Expected signatures: Panasonic AEHA leader about 3.45-3.5 ms / 1.7 ms, then 40 bits (83 edges), trailer, then about 75 ms gap and the identical frame again. Hitachi AEHA uses the same leader with 88 bits (179 edges). NEC lighting uses a 9-10 ms / 4.5-5 ms leader, 32 bits and a stop bit, with 9 ms / 2.25 ms repeat codes while held. Iris uses a two-mark leader (about 2.1 / 0.95 / 5.5 / 0.96 ms) and pulse-WIDTH bits. PITFALLS: (1) Receivers stretch marks and shrink spaces by 50-150 us, so classify by mark/space ratio. One NEC remote measured 10.15/5.0 ms with 650-700 us marks. (2) Buffer and timeout: IRremoteESP8266's default buffer of about 100 entries is too small for 88-bit frames (179 edges). Use >= 512 and a timeout that splits frames at the 47-75 ms gaps; keep one frame and record the repeat count and gap. IRremoteESP8266 labels 40-bit Panasonic-lighting frames UNKNOWN '42 bits'. Arduino-IRremote shows them as PulseDistance; Flipper stores RAW. (3) Several remotes send each press 2 times (Panasonic, Takizumi). When replaying, send the frame twice with the observed gap. Held keys send repeats (NEC repeat codes, or full AEHA frames about every 130 ms). (4) Toggles vs discrete: Panasonic, NEC and Toshiba have discrete 全灯/消灯. Iris cycles 点灯 -> 常夜灯 -> 消灯 on one key [docs: ELPA footnote]. Takizumi and no-name lamps use 入/切 toggles, and NEC's AB key is an ON/OFF toggle. Learn discrete keys first and track state for toggles. (5) Carrier: AEHA allows 33-40 kHz (38 typ). Every lighting remote found is consistent with 38 kHz, duty about 1/3. A 38 kHz demodulator still receives 36-40 kHz at reduced range, so a learned signal never tells you the exact carrier; transmit at 38 kHz. (6) Unit T varies by maker (Panasonic about 432-450, Hitachi about 400-450, one Sharp-branded lamp needed 390). Prefer replaying measured timings over re-synthesising with a textbook T. (7) Lamps fade on and off over about 3 s [docs: Toshiba/NVC manual], so wait at least 3-4 s before judging with a camera or light sensor. (8) Channel: factory default is CH1 for lamp and remote [docs: Toshiba/NVC manual]. A remote set to CH2/CH3 sends different codes (Panasonic bits 3-4 of the command byte, NEC bit 7), so learn the user's actual remote as-is. (9) Notation: normalise every capture to transmission-order LSB-first bytes before storing (see conventions).
searchCandidateOrder: 0. Precondition: lamp ON at full brightness via the wall switch (most lamps restore the last or full state). Camera or lux sensor watching it; Cardputer IR (or Unit IR on G2) aimed at the lamp's receiver window in the centre of the fixture, ideally under 2-3 m. Send OFF candidates first, because ON->OFF is the most visible discrete change. After each send wait about 4 s, then confirm a hit with the matching 全灯/点灯 code.
1. Panasonic CH1 消灯: AEHA T=432, 2C 52 09 2F 26, sent 2 times about 75 ms apart; confirm with 全灯 2C 52 09 2C 25
2. NEC/HotaluX CH1 消灯: NEC 82 6D BE 41; confirm with 全灯 82 6D A6 59 or 82 6D BD 42
3. Toshiba(NVC) CH1 消灯: NEC E7 0C 8B 74; confirm with 点灯 E7 0C A2 5D (also covers some Daiko)
4. Hitachi 消灯: AEHA 88-bit 01 10 30 50 AF 00 FF 03 FC C2 3D at T=425, then T=390 (also covers the Sharp-branded case); confirm only via 保安灯 01 10 30 50 AF 00 FF 09 F6 C2 3D (全灯 unknown)
5. Iris Ohyama 5.x/6.x cycle key (proprietary PWM, MSB-first C0 81 40 00 5B): expect ON -> 常夜灯; low confidence when synthesised
6. Takizumi 入/切 toggle: NEC 84 52 32 CD, sent 2 times about 47 ms apart; then NEC 84 51 2A D5 (unidentified, possibly Odelic)
7. Repeat steps 1-2 on other channels: Panasonic CH2 2C 52 09 37 3E, CH3 2C 52 09 3F 36; NEC CH2 82 6D 3E C1

8. If nothing reacts: Koizumi, Odelic, Daiko, Sharp, Mitsubishi and OEM brands have no public codes. Ask the user for the brand or remote model printed on the remote, or learn the remote with the Unit IR receiver (the most reliable path).

NEVER sweep unknown command bytes: they include channel-programming and memory keys (Panasonic チャンネル確定 2C 52 39 DA-DC; Toshiba メモリ+全灯 moves the lamp to CH2), which can leave the lamp deaf to its own remote.

doNotSend.what: Unknown command bytes in a known family (NEC 82 6D xx, E7 0C xx, AEHA 2C 52 39 xx) may be memory or channel-set keys

risks: Coverage: only Panasonic and NEC/HotaluX are well documented. Toshiba has on/off only, Hitachi one model (no 全灯), Iris several proprietary formats, and Koizumi/Odelic/Daiko/Sharp/Mitsubishi none. A blind search can therefore fail; plan for learning with the Unit IR receiver.
Model variance inside a brand: Panasonic uses system nibble 0 vs 3; NEC power keys A6, AB or BD; Iris has 4 ELPA code families.
Bit-order and notation mismatches between libraries (LSB-first bytes, IRremote little-endian words, ESPHome/IRremoteESP8266/telecotele MSB-first). A wrong byte order fails silently.
Decoder gaps: 40-bit Panasonic, 88-bit Hitachi and Iris pulse-width frames are not standard Kaseikyo-48 or NEC, so transmit raw mark/space arrays (RMT) rather than relying on a library protocol.
IR power and aim: the Cardputer's built-in LED is weak (an ATtiny Panasonic build only worked at about 50 cm), so aim at the receiver or use the Unit IR.
State and timing: 3 s fades, toggles, the night-light state, and wall-switch power-cycling modes. Detection logic must wait and track state.
Safety: never brute-force unknown commands (channel and memory keys).
